It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Alice Springs, Australia at 2026-11-10 18:27 ACST (UTC+0930) (2026-11-10T08:57:00Z in UTC), at latitude -23.698 degrees and longitude 133.8807 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 5.086 degrees and its azimuth is 253.378 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 16.793 degrees and its azimuth is 249.764 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 1.32 percent illuminated, 13.169 degrees from the Sun, and 398861.4 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Probably not—despite the Moon being geometrically above the horizon.

At your stated time, the Moon is only **1.32% illuminated** and just **13.2° from the Sun**. That means it is an extremely thin crescent, with the illuminated portion facing toward the Sun and likely only a few tens of arcminutes across in apparent width. Although its altitude is 16.8°, the bright daytime sky and the Sun’s altitude of 5.1° still create substantial glare and contrast loss. The Moon’s azimuth is also only about 3.6° from the Sun’s, so it is in nearly the same part of the sky.

An experienced observer using binoculars or a telescope—and taking strict precautions to avoid the Sun—might detect it under favorable atmospheric conditions. But for an ordinary unaided observer, even knowing where to look, it would be **very unlikely to see**, and it may be effectively invisible in the bright sky.

So your hope is reasonable: **you probably would not be able to spot it with the naked eye.** Never scan near the Sun with binoculars or a telescope; accidental direct viewing can cause permanent eye damage.
